The following parts refer to a motor vehicle: its early Australian-built body and safety features, its hydraulic braking system, and a hydraulic cylinder system used to operate it.
The sketch shows an early Australian-built car.
Explain how TWO features of this early Australian-built car have been modified in modern cars to improve their safety.
Only features visible in the sketch earn marks — the rounded body with separate mudguards and running boards, the pillar-mounted windscreen, the exposed bumper bar, the spoked wheels, the open cabin without restraints.
For each feature name what a modern car uses instead and then say what that change does in a collision. ‘Better’ or a safer-sounding word on its own is not an explanation of how safety is improved.
The diagram represents part of a car's hydraulic braking system.
Outline the operation of this hydraulic system and its advantages over mechanical systems.
Trace the force path in order — pedal, linkage, master cylinder piston, pressurised fluid, line, caliper piston, pads, disc. The marks are for the sequence and the cause of each step, not for a list of the parts you can see.
Then state the advantages against a mechanical system specifically: fewer parts to maintain, force multiplication from the ratio of piston areas, and a sealed fluid link that transmits the force directly. Do not restate the operation as though it were an advantage.

The following parts refer to a simple radio receiver: its circuit, the influence of semiconductors on telecommunications product design, and the documentation drawing of a radio aerial support bracket.
A circuit diagram of a simple radio receiver is shown.
Name the components labelled $A$ and $B$ and outline each component's function in this circuit.
Start from where each component sits in the circuit. The component in series with the tuned circuit can conduct on one half of the cycle only — that behaviour is what tells you its name and its job.
The component in shunt (parallel) with the loudspeaker provides a low-impedance path that diverts part of the signal away from the loudspeaker. Ask what would still be reaching the loudspeaker if that component were not there.
Each mark pair is a name plus a function, so give them in that order and do not describe the function before naming the component.
How have semi-conductors influenced the design of modern telecommunications products?
The question asks about the design of the product, so answer with what the designer can now do or make better — not with how a semiconductor behaves electrically.
Think about how telecommunications products have changed over the last few decades: their size, their mass, how long the battery lasts, how fast they respond, how much function is packed in, and how well they survive being dropped or knocked.
Two distinct design consequences are needed for the full marks; two versions of the same idea is only one.
A radio aerial support bracket bolted to a steel plate is shown. Complete a fully sectioned front view of the bracket assembly. Apply AS1100.
Construct the view from the given top view first — project every visible edge — and only then decide what cutting plane A-A actually cuts.
In a full section, everything between the viewer and the cutting plane is removed, so hidden detail behind the plane is not drawn and only the cut faces are hatched.
Hatch at $45^{\circ}$ with even spacing of about $1.5$–$2\,\mathrm{mm}$ and change the angle or spacing for each adjacent part; add centre lines on the post and bolt axes and apply the correct line weights.

The following parts refer to a telephone charger: the material of its electrical pins, the manufacture of its polymer cover, and the digitisation of the voice signal it belongs to.
Contrast the key features of fixed and mobile telephone systems.
Build the answer as matched pairs — one feature of the fixed system with the opposite feature of the mobile system beside it — rather than as two separate descriptions that never meet.
The strongest contrast is the transmission medium itself; interference, dropout, bandwidth, security and the locations that can be served all follow from it, so start there and derive the rest.
A smart-phone transmits digital information. One step in this process is to convert analogue voice data to digitised data.
Outline how an analogue signal is digitised using *sampling* and *quantising*.
The analogue wave is continuous in two independent ways — in time and in amplitude — and digitising removes each continuity by a different mechanism.
Decide which of the two terms deals with the intervals between readings and which deals with the number of discrete levels a reading may take, and say what each one produces on the lower graph.

The following parts refer to light aircraft: the choice of propulsion system, the control adjustments that vary lift, a wind tunnel test of an aerofoil, and non-destructive testing of aircraft components.
The two images show light aircraft powered by different propulsion systems.
Identify a suitable propulsion system for each aircraft and justify your choice.
Identify the engine type for each aircraft from the drawings: look for jet intakes and a jet exhaust on one, and a nose-mounted propeller on the other.
Then justify: what does each class of aircraft actually need from its engine? Consider speed and range for one of them, and runway length, purchase cost and maintenance sophistication for the other.
A justification that only says 'jets are fast' is incomplete - tie the engine type to a specific operating requirement of that class of aircraft.
Outline TWO control adjustments that can be made to vary the lift force acting on an aircraft during flight.
Lift depends on three things: the angle the wing is set at, how fast the wing is moving through the air, and how much wing area there is. Each of the three can be adjusted.
One of them is limited: beyond a maximum angle of attack of about $15^{\circ}$ the flow separates from the wing and lift is lost, so angle of attack cannot simply be increased indefinitely.
Aim to name TWO distinct adjustments, and for each one say which of the three quantities it changes.
An aerofoil was tested in a wind tunnel.
This test produced a resultant force of $350\,\mathrm{N}$ at an angle of $10^{\circ}$ to the lift axis.
Calculate the lift to drag ratio.
The 350 N is the resultant of the lift and the drag, inclined at $10^{\circ}$ to the lift axis - it is not the lift itself.
Resolve the resultant: the component along the lift axis is the lift, and the component perpendicular to it is the drag.
Form the ratio as lift divided by drag, then quote it with the smaller quantity written first. Watch the degree mode on your calculator.
Outline the ultrasonic testing process and its advantages for use in testing aircraft components.
Two things are required: how the test actually works, and what makes it worth using on aircraft components.
For the process, think in terms of a sound wave being sent into the component and something coming back. A flaw in the material changes both what returns and how quickly it returns.
For the advantages, consider what a maintenance technician does NOT have to do to an aircraft under this test, compared with a test that requires the part to be removed or cut open.

covers the historical development of communication devices, methods of generating electricity, and a sectioned front view drawn to AS 1100 standards.

How has each of these devices contributed to the advancement of telecommunications?
Take the devices in the order they are shown and, for each, name the specific capability it added — a new way of sending a signal, a new medium, or a new set of functions carried by a single device.
Keep the three contributions different in kind. If two of them are really the same idea written differently, only one mark is earned for the pair.
Describe TWO methods of generating electricity.
Describe each method as a chain: energy source → conversion device → electrical output, and choose two routes that start from different sources, such as a fuel-driven rotating generator and a light-driven or moving-mass-driven one.
Characteristics earn the marks, not just names: the heat source used, what turns the generator, what the output is used for, and one advantage or limitation of each route.

This diagram shows the cross-section of a highway pavement drawn using AS 1100 drawing standards.
This diagram shows the cross-section of a highway pavement drawn using AS 1100 drawing standards.
Explain the benefits of using AS 1100 drawing standards in the preparation of engineering drawings such as the one above.
AS 1100 is a standard for how drawings are made and communicated, so think about the consequences of two people interpreting the same drawing differently.
Standards also decide conventions: Australia projects in first angle while much of the world uses third angle, so a standard removes that ambiguity too.
The question says explain, so attach the benefit to each reason rather than listing reasons on their own.
A heavy vehicle is travelling on a level section of the highway at a constant velocity of $90\,\mathrm{km/h}$ while experiencing a resistance to motion of $18\,\mathrm{kN}$.
Calculate the power required to maintain this velocity.
At constant velocity the acceleration is zero, so the tractive force from the engine exactly balances the resistance, and the power is just force times speed.
Convert the speed to metres per second before multiplying, then check the unit you get out of $F \times v$.
Sanity check the magnitude: $18\,\mathrm{kN}$ at $25\,\mathrm{m/s}$ gives a power of order $10^{5}\,\mathrm{W}$.

An image of a truck is shown.
An image of a truck is shown.
Compare the selection of laminated glass with toughened glass as a windscreen for this vehicle.
This is a comparison of two windscreens for the same job, so treat them in the same order: shared properties first, then the difference in fracture behaviour, then cost, weight and fabrication.
Ask what must not happen when the screen is struck: the driver must not be thrown out and must not be cut by fragments.
Note that does not shatter into dangerous fragments and keeps its shape and stays see-through when cracked are different properties, and each glass type has only one of them.
Give reasons for selecting an aluminium alloy for the side panel of the truck.
Answer in terms of the loads the panel must carry (its own mass, cargo and any impact) against its cost, and remember that a truck side panel is a large, thin, shaped, exposed surface.
Also consider the environment: the panel is exposed to weather and road splash, and it has to be produced in large flat or curved shapes and attached to the chassis.
The marks want a strength-type property plus a second, unrelated reason — two versions of the same idea is only one mark.
Truck tyres are made using vulcanised synthetic rubber combined with high tensile steel wire.
Explain why this combination of materials has been chosen.
Do not just list properties. The question asks why the two materials are used together, so the answer must be about what each one does that the other cannot.
Consider the loads on a tyre: vertical load, impact from kerbs and potholes, and the forces that try to squash or spread the sidewall.
Remember what a rubber casing with no reinforcement would do at speed, and what would be lost if the steel were used alone.
A mild steel nut and bolt is used to hold a bumper bar onto the chassis of the truck. The bolt needs to withstand a maximum shear load of $2\,\mathrm{kN}$.
If the maximum shear stress of the material is $56\,\mathrm{MPa}$ and the factor of safety is $2$, calculate the minimum bolt diameter.
The factor of safety is applied to the strength, not to the load: halve the maximum shear stress to obtain the stress this bolt may safely carry.
Decide how many shear planes the bolt has at this joint. A single bolt passing through the bumper bar and the chassis is in single shear, with one shear plane across the shank, so use the full circular cross-section rather than half of it.
Solve for $d^{2}$ before taking the square root, and finish with the diameter in millimetres.

concerns a small drone: how it achieves flight, the manufacture of its nylon and carbon fibre composite propellers, aircraft flight control systems, and the aerodynamic drag of an aerofoil compared with a taut cable.
Aircraft flight control systems use either cables or 'fly-by-wire' systems.
Contrast these flight control systems.
A contrast needs both sides: a feature of one system, the matching or opposing feature of the other, and at least one thing the two have in common.
Trace the path of a single pilot input through each system, from the stick to the control surface, and note every stage that can fail, add mass or add friction.
Think about what each system gives the pilot back: one is immediate, mechanical and tactile; the other is processed, computed and possibly augmented.
A taut cable and aerofoil of similar thickness are tested in a wind tunnel. The results show that the aerofoil produces significantly less drag than the cable.
Explain how the aerofoil produces less drag than the taut cable. Use the diagram to assist your response.
Compare the two bodies the same way: what shape is each one, and what happens to the air immediately behind it?
Drag is set by two things — how much low pressure the body leaves in its wake, and how much friction its surface creates — and both are decided by the shape of the rear of the body and the roughness of its surface.
Annotate the empty flow region of the diagram with streamlines and with the separation and vortex region for each body; that annotated diagram is part of what is being marked.

A simplified diagram of a pin jointed truss of a hammerhead crane is shown. It is lifting a load of $54\,\mathrm{kN}$.
What are redundant truss members?
Define redundancy relative to the load case, not to the member itself: ask what force the member carries for the loading shown, and whether the truss would behave identically with that member removed.
The full mark needs both the zero-force statement and the qualification that a different loading can make the same member load-carrying.
The structural steel I-beams used to make the crane were hot-rolled then normalised.
Explain why normalising was chosen as the heat treatment process. Support your answer with a labelled sketch of the resulting microstructure.
Normalising reheats the steel into the austenite range and then cools it in still air, so the cooling rate sits between furnace cooling and quenching. Think about what that does to grain size, and therefore to strength and toughness.
A crane beam has to be strong without becoming brittle or expensive, so the justification is about gaining adequate strength economically and relieving residual stress. The sketch has to show the grain size the process produces, and it must be labelled.

The table compares the $\mathrm{CO_2}$ emissions of three transport systems – car, train and aircraft.
The table shows that these transport systems produce different amounts of $\mathrm{CO_2}$ emissions per passenger.
Why are these different transport systems still required?
The answer is about choice, not about emissions. No single mode can do everything, so the different systems are each the best option for particular journeys.
One mark is for naming a valid reason and one is for explaining how that reason justifies keeping more than one system. A bare list of reasons earns one mark only.
For each transport system shown in the $\mathrm{CO_2}$ emissions table, explain how an engineering innovation in that transport system has affected the environment.
Three transport systems and seven marks means a different, well explained innovation for each. Using the same innovation in all three will not earn three separate explanations.
For each system, complete the chain: the innovation, the mechanism by which it works, the change in fuel or energy use, and the resulting effect on the environment. Marks are given for the explanation, not for the name.
For the aircraft, look at where the thrust actually comes from: a large proportion of the air passing through the engine is never burnt, which is why engine efficiency improved so dramatically.

A fidget spinner is shown. It is a toy that contains a ball bearing in its centre and is designed to spin on its axis with little effort.
The central components of a fidget spinner are press fitted together using a press punch.
The press punch diameter is $21\,\mathrm{mm}$. The force applied by the press punch to the bearing is $17.3\,\mathrm{N}$. Calculate the compressive stress in the press punch.
The punch is loaded in compression, so the stress is the applied force spread evenly over the circular face of the punch: $\sigma = F/a$.
Convert the diameter to metres before you compute the area ($21\,\mathrm{mm} = 21\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m}$). If the area is left in square millimetres the answer comes out in the wrong unit by a factor of $10^{6}$.
The body of the fidget spinner is made from polypropylene. The bearing is made from steel. When the force $P$ applied by the press punch is $16\,\mathrm{N}$, the bearing slides into position. Calculate the normal force $N$ acting on the bearing walls if the coefficient of friction between polypropylene and steel is $0.20$.
The bearing is just beginning to slide, so the friction between the polypropylene wall and the steel bearing has reached its limiting value: $F = \mu N$.
In that relationship the force along the surface of contact is the press force driving the bearing in, and the unknown is the force pressing the walls outward. Rearranging the relationship makes the normal force the subject.
The top view of a fidget spinner is shown.
What force $Q$ is required to overcome the $20\,\mathrm{N}$ resistance force shown?
Treat the bearing as the pivot. The $20\,\mathrm{N}$ resistance acts through the bearing, so it has no moment about the bearing axis, and only $Q$ produces a turning moment.
The view is drawn to scale, so measure the perpendicular distance from the centre of the bearing to the line of action of $Q$ on the figure, and measure the moment arm of the $20\,\mathrm{N}$ force the same way. Keep both in the same units before substituting.
Sanity check: $Q$ is applied further out from the axis than the resisting force, so it should come out smaller than $20\,\mathrm{N}$.

The photograph shows a board with a hydrofoil attached underneath. The hydrofoil is used to lift the board out of the water as the rider is towed behind a boat at high speed. Explain why the hydrofoil can lift the board out of the water when it is travelling at high speed.

addresses telecommunications engineering: a telecommunications innovation, a logic circuit, an orthographic production drawing and the properties of electrolytic tough pitch (ETP) copper.
Outline how ONE telecommunications engineering innovation has influenced traditional voice communication systems.
Choose ONE innovation and stay with it. A response that names several inventions without explaining any of them scores the lower band only.
Structure it as a chain: the innovation, then what it changed about the way voice is carried (the network, the switching, the cost, the reach), then the consequence for the user or the provider.
Valid examples include the mobile cellular network, VoIP and internet telephony, the private branch exchange, and the smartphone or cloud service that has replaced the landline.
The diagram shows a simple logic circuit with inputs $A$, $B$, $C$ and $D$, and output $Z$.
Inputs $A$ and $D$ are set to 'high' ($1$). Determine, using the logic circuit diagram, the combination of inputs at $B$ and $C$ which will produce a high ($1$) output at $Z$. Use the truth table to support your answer.
Build the table one gate at a time. Write the output of the AND gate and the output of the OR gate on separate intermediate rows before filling in $Z$.
Remember the defining behaviour of the last gate: a NOR output is high only when both of its inputs are low, while a NAND output is high only when both of its inputs are high.
Use the completed column as a check. With $A$ and $D$ already high, one of the intermediate outputs can never be low, which is a useful warning that the printed circuit cannot do what the question asks.
The following drawing provides a series of orthographic views of a machine part, supported by a 'modified' title block. Some of the features have been labelled with the numbers 4 to 10.
With reference to the orthographic views and the modified title block, complete the table below.
Read the title block first: it tells you the standard, the units, the tolerance, the scale and the projection method, and several of the blanks come straight from it.
Name each view from the way it was produced: a view taken through a cutting plane is a section, a view projected perpendicular to an inclined face is an auxiliary view, and the projection symbol decides first or third angle.
Use the standard names for the numbered features: alternating short and long dashes are hidden detail, fine diagonal lining on a cut face is cross-hatching, and a hole that is enlarged and deepened to take a fastener head is a counterbore.
Electrolytic tough pitch (ETP) copper has many desirable properties that support its use in telecommunications. In the table, provide an explanation for the importance of each of the listed properties of ETP copper.
Each explanation must link the property to what it allows the cable to do in a telecommunications network, so finish every sentence with the consequence.
Start with the conductor: the signal is an electric current in a long, thin wire, so think about resistance, and about the cross-section and length of the conductor.
Then think about installation and lifetime: cables are drawn through ducts, laid in the ground or hung on poles, and are expected to keep working for decades with little maintenance.

questions.text:
addresses aeronautical engineering: an innovation that improved aircraft performance, wing materials over the last 100 years, a non-destructive airworthiness test and a fluid-force calculation.
Outline how ONE innovation in aeronautical engineering has contributed to improved performance of modern aircraft.
Only ONE innovation, and the marks need the link to a performance gain: name it, say what it changed, then give the benefit.
Acceptable areas include wingtip devices, higher-bypass turbofans, composite structures, fly-by-wire and satellite navigation.
A performance gain can be speed, range, fuel burn, payload, reliability or safety. Pick one and be quantitative if you can — saying only that it is better is half the answer.
Describe the use of different types of materials for the wings of aircraft over the last 100 years.
The question covers the last 100 years, so the answer must be a sequence: name each era's material in the order it was used.
For each era, state what the change bought — strength, stiffness, weight, speed, span or cost — not just the name of the material.
Both the wing skin and the internal frame or spar are acceptable, but pick one and be consistent rather than switching between them.
A periodic aircraft maintenance inspection is to be carried out. Identify and justify an appropriate test that could be used to check the airworthiness of the landing gear.
The method must be non-destructive — the landing gear must still be airworthy afterwards, so anything that requires cutting, drilling or stressing the component is excluded.
The defect being hunted for in a heavily loaded leg is a fatigue or sub-surface crack that has not yet reached the surface, so choose a method that penetrates the material rather than one that only reads the surface.
A full answer justifies the choice twice: why the method suits the defect, and why it suits the inspection situation (in situ, portable, no damage).
An air gauge contains air at $750\,\mathrm{kPa}$ (gauge) while atmospheric pressure is at $100\,\mathrm{kPa}$. The air at absolute pressure operates a piston of $15\,\mathrm{mm}$ diameter.
Calculate the force the compressed air exerts on the piston.
The pressure is labelled gauge, and gauge pressure is measured relative to the atmosphere. The force on the piston is set by the pressure inside the cylinder, so the atmospheric pressure has to be accounted for.
Draw the piston as a free body: the internal pressure pushes down on the piston face while the atmosphere pushes up on the other side, so the net force uses the absolute pressure inside the cylinder.
Keep the diameter in metres when computing the area so that pressure in pascals multiplied by area in square metres gives a force in newtons, with no conversion step left at the end.

questions.text:
addresses civil structures and public works: a cast concrete pad, stainless steel yokes, a turnbuckle pin and the AS 1100 front view of the assembly.
A photograph of a cast concrete pad is shown.
Describe why concrete would have been selected for this situation.
The pad is cast, so start with the property that makes concrete suitable for a compressive load, and then with the property that makes it suitable for being cast into this shape.
Consider where the pad is being made: it has to follow an anchor point, it is partly embedded, and it must sit on an existing base.
Include a point about how the material is strengthened where tension is present, and one about durability outdoors, if you can.
The photograph shows two stainless steel yokes which attach a turnbuckle to a baseplate fixed to a concrete pad.
Provide a step-by-step description of an appropriate method to manufacture the yoke.
The yoke is a low-volume, thin, stainless steel part, so the process is a sheet-metal process — not casting, and not machining from solid.
Keep the sequence of operations straight: the shape is first produced essentially flat by removing material, then the depth is developed by forming, then the edges are finished.
Naming the right operations in the correct order is what earns the third mark; the same operations listed out of order score only the 2-mark band.
The photograph shows a turnbuckle and yoke secured by a pin.
The diameter of the pin in the turnbuckle is $40\,\mathrm{mm}$ and the shear stress across this pin is $55\,\mathrm{MPa}$.
Find the magnitude of the axial load on the turnbuckle.
Count the shear planes before anything else. A clevis pin is in double shear, because the load is carried on two cross-sections of the pin rather than one.
So the shear stress acts on twice the cross-sectional area, and the axial load is twice the single-shear value you get from $\sigma = F/A$.
Keep the diameter in metres so the stress in pascals gives a force in newtons, then convert to kilonewtons for the final answer.
An exploded view of a yoke and turnbuckle is shown.
Complete the assembled front view in the space below. Apply AS 1100 drawing standards. Do NOT show hidden detail. Do NOT add dimensions. Scale $1:2$.
Read the FRONT arrow on the exploded isometric and project onto a plane square to it. Only one view is required, so there is no first-angle or third-angle decision to make.
Only edges visible from that direction are drawn, and hidden detail is explicitly not required, so do not attempt it — marks are lost if you add it.
Remember the stated scale of 1:2, add no dimensions, and put a centre line on the axis of the threaded rod and the clevis pin.

covers professional obligations, hot working processes for riveted steel trusses, and a truss force calculation.
Describe potential legal and ethical implications of a professional engineer failing to undertake ongoing training.
Answer from both sides: what the engineer could be held to under the law, and what they owe to the public under the code of ethics.
Being current is about more than design skills. Think about work health and safety obligations and about the currency of the standards the engineer signs off against.
Consequences run both ways: to the engineer's own registration and career, and to the people who rely on the design.
Members of steel trusses are often connected using metal rivets as shown.
Describe the hot working process that the rivet has undergone to create the resulting structure. Support your answer by completing and labelling the diagram of the sectioned rivet.
Hot working means the metal is deformed well above its recrystallisation temperature, so say what the temperature has to be above and why that matters.
The completed section must show what the grains do around the formed head, not just the outline of the head.
Keep hot working and heat treatment apart: one changes the shape of the component, the other changes its properties.
A cycle bridge has been constructed using a Warren girder truss loaded as shown. The diagram is drawn to scale.
By considering necessary loads and reactions, calculate the magnitude and the nature of the force in member $C$.
The diagram is drawn to scale, so measure it. The diagonals of a Warren girder of this proportion meet the chord at $60^{\circ}$, and the truss height is $2 \times 0.866 = 1.732$ member lengths.
Start with the reactions. Taking moments about the pin support removes the vertical reaction and the horizontal reaction there, leaving the roller reaction.
The $3\,\mathrm{kN}$ load acts along the top chord, so it has no vertical component. After the reactions, a section cutting the top chord, member C and the bottom chord lets you use $\sum F_y$ on the right-hand piece to isolate the vertical component of the force in C.

questions.text:
covers corrosion protection of civil structures, digital signal transmission, receiving antenna signal strength and DC traction motor control.
Describe methods used to protect civil structures against corrosion. Support your answer with examples.
Two broad approaches protect a steel structure: keep the corrosive agents away from the surface, or make the structure the cathode so that any corrosion happens somewhere else.
Each method needs an example, and the example has to be named precisely - a specific structure or component, not just the metal.
Describe the mechanism, not the name: how the coating works, or which metal corrodes instead of the structure and what happens to it when it is used up.
Outline benefits of digital signal transmission.
Compare digital with analogue: in an analogue system every noise disturbance along the path stays in the signal, but in a digital system the receiver decides only whether each pulse is a 1 or a 0.
Follow the signal down a long cable and ask what happens to it. Does its amplitude keep shrinking and keep picking up noise, or is it read and rebuilt along the way?
Once you realise the signal is really data, list the extra things that become possible because of that: secrecy, several signals sharing one path, error checking, and later processing or storage.
Discuss methods for increasing the signal strength of a receiving antenna.
The question says 'discuss', so for each method you raise, say what it achieves and what its drawback is. A method with no drawback scores only partially.
For one method, ask what happens to the unwanted part of the signal when it is turned up - anything that is amplified along with the wanted signal is amplified too.
For another, think about the geometry of the aerial itself: its length relative to the wavelength of the wanted signal, and how widely it radiates.
The diagram shows an electrical circuit that is used to control the speed of a DC electric traction motor.
Explain, with reference to the diagram, how the speed of the motor can be controlled.
Ask first what determines the speed of a DC motor, and what actually limits the current when it starts.
Look at how the four resistors are connected: each one has a switch across it, so each switch can take its resistor out of the circuit.
Then follow the current path. Fewer resistors in series means less total resistance, so a larger share of the supply voltage reaches the armature, and a larger armature current means more torque and a higher speed. Remember that at start the motor's back EMF is zero, which is why the resistors are needed at all.

addresses engineering communication and graphics: the reason for AS 1100 production drawing standards and the production of a pictorial drawing.
Explain why engineering production drawings prepared for Australian use should adhere to AS 1100 drawing standards.
AS 1100 is a communication standard, not a design standard, so the answer is about what happens when a drawing is read by someone who did not draw it.
Two things are needed for a drawing to be unambiguous: one agreed set of conventions, and a way of checking that a drawing has been prepared correctly. Think about who pays for a manufacturing mistake.
An orthographic drawing of a toggle switch is shown.
Produce a pictorial drawing of the toggle switch when viewed from the direction indicated by arrow A. Use a scale of $2:1$.
This part asks for a pictorial, that is a three dimensional representation, not one more orthographic view. An isometric or an auxiliary projection made from the given views is what is wanted.
A pictorial cannot be scaled off a single view. The standard method is to construct an auxiliary view in the direction of arrow A, then rotate it into 3D using a 45 degree mitre line and a true length scale line.
The 2:1 scale doubles every dimension, and anything that is curved or polygonal in the orthographic views must be drawn as a curve or a true polygon in the pictorial rather than as a straight line.

This question concerns long-term aircraft storage, aircraft safety, aircraft propulsion and composite aircraft materials.
Due to a reduction in air travel, an airline company has had to store some of its unused aircraft.
Explain why the desert is a suitable place to store the unused aircraft.
Start with the material the airframe is made from and the mechanism by which it deteriorates, then find the climate that prevents it. Modern carbon fibre airframes do not corrode, so the corrosion argument belongs to the aluminium-alloy airframes that make up most stored fleets.
The decisive points are moisture and heat: crevice corrosion in the lap joints between aluminium sheets and galvanic corrosion between dissimilar metals both need water to proceed, so low humidity, almost no rainfall and a climate that dries out crevices are the key reasons. Other creditable points: much lower storage cost away from an airport, hard dry ground that needs no paving, no birds or insects nesting in the airframe or engines, and low humidity protecting the engines and avionics.
How has the work of aeronautical engineers helped to improve aircraft safety?
For full marks, name several specific safety features and say how each one removes a risk. 'Better safety' or 'more reliable aircraft' earns nothing.
Strong contributions to draw on: built-in redundancy in flight systems and computers, so a single failure is survivable; autopilot and autoland at major airports, which reduce workload and pilot error while keeping the pilot informed; stronger and lighter materials giving more robust airframes and better crash survivability; cockpit vigilance devices; remanent life and fatigue analysis; and maintenance completed to the manufacturer's specification.
A $3000\,\mathrm{kg}$ aircraft is flying in level flight at constant speed.
Using a free-body diagram, calculate the thrust on the plane if the lift to drag ratio of the aircraft is $11 : 1$.
kN
Draw the free-body diagram first: four forces, and in level flight at constant speed they balance, so lift equals weight and thrust equals drag.
The lift to drag ratio is a ratio of two forces, so once the lift is known from the weight the drag follows, and the thrust equals the drag. Keep the units consistent and give the answer in the units of the answer line (kN).
Carbon fibre epoxy is an example of a composite material used in aircraft construction.
Describe the benefits of using this composite in aircraft construction in terms of both its manufacturing properties and its in-service properties.
The question asks for two different things - how the material is made, and how it behaves once it is in service. Keep the two sets of points separate and make sure at least one point appears in each.
Manufacturing: a resin matrix with fibres can be laid up and cured into strong, complex shapes that would be difficult to form or machine in metal, and the layup is repeatable from a CAD definition. In service: higher strength and stiffness at lower mass than the metal it replaces, so either fuel consumption falls or payload rises; and the strength can be anisotropic, different along and across the fibres, or made more nearly isotropic by varying the layup.

A telecommunications engineer is designing a Wi-Fi network that will use either a $2.4\,\mathrm{GHz}$ or $5\,\mathrm{GHz}$ signal in a client's local area network.
How do the $2.4\,\mathrm{GHz}$ and $5\,\mathrm{GHz}$ signals differ in performance?
Decide what performance means for a wireless link: how much data is delivered per second, and how much of the transmitted signal is lost on the way.
The 5 GHz band is the higher frequency. Higher frequency radio is scattered and absorbed more strongly by walls, glass and moisture, so the same transmitter power gives a usable signal over a shorter distance and through fewer obstacles.
That is the penalty. Now look at the other side: the 5 GHz band is much less crowded than 2.4 GHz, so more channel width is available in it and a higher data rate is possible.
Outline how voltage can be tested in a circuit.
The instrument has to be connected so that it measures the difference in potential between two points, not the current flowing through one point — that means across the component, in parallel, not in series.
The instrument's own resistance must be very much greater than the resistance of the circuit, otherwise connecting it changes the current being measured. On a multimeter the range must also be set high enough to avoid a short circuit or an over-range reading.
Describe the basic principles of low orbit satellite telecommunication systems.
There are two facts on which a low orbit system depends: how long a satellite takes to complete one orbit, and how long that satellite can see one handset.
Put those two numbers together — a few minutes of useful time out of a 90 minute orbit — and work out why so many satellites are needed and why a handover mechanism is essential.

questions.text:
This question concerns aeronautical engineering design and technical communication: the use of computer graphics in aeronautical engineering, the benefits of collaboration when completing the engineering report, a freehand isometric sketch of an aircraft wing rib constructed from orthogonal views, and the microstructure of a thermosetting polymer. Answer parts (a) to (d).
How can computer graphics be utilised as a tool in aeronautical engineering?
The question is asking for named aeronautical applications, not a general statement about computers. Think about what an aeronautical engineer needs to do before a prototype exists.
Test each point you write by asking what the engineer actually does with it: testing a change before manufacturing it, or showing the client something that does not exist yet.
You are part of a team of engineers working collaboratively on the design of a new aircraft.
Explain the benefits of collaboration when completing the engineering report.
Answer for the whole report, not just the writing-up stage: research, data collection, testing, analysis, drafting, review and compilation.
Use cause and effect in every point — say what the team does and what results from it, e.g. 'a second engineer checks the calculations, so an error is less likely to reach the client'.
An orthogonal view of a rib in an aircraft wing is shown.
Construct a freehand isometric sketch of the wing rib as viewed in the direction of the arrow.
Only isometric lines will earn marks here: every receding edge at 30° to the horizontal and all vertical edges truly vertical. Oblique, perspective or planometric drawings do not satisfy this question.
Use the view that shows the rib's true profile for the outline and the side view for its thickness. Remember that a circle drawn on edge appears as an ellipse in an isometric sketch.
Draw, label and describe the microstructure of a thermosetting polymer.
The key idea is cross-linking: think about what holds neighbouring polymer chains together, and about what that does when the material is reheated.
A labelled network of chains plus two or three properties (rigid or hard, does not soften when heated, cannot be remelted) will pick up the description marks.

Describe the responsibilities of the engineer when considering security issues of telecommunications devices.
Frame each point as a duty: what could go wrong to the network or to the consumer's data, and what the engineer does to prevent it.

Compare the properties of the two materials in roller coaster support structures.

A full answer needs at least one property that favours steel and one that favours timber, each tied to a consequence for the support structure.

The diagram shows a partially completed microstructure of the parent and weld metals.

Draw and label the three types in the heat-affected zone of ONE web only, and put the labels on leader lines pointing at the right regions.
A roller coaster car is at rest at point A as shown.

questions.text:
This question concerns aeronautical manufacturing, electronics, telecommunications and mechanics: the compression moulding of aircraft components, the functions of a transistor in an electrical circuit, how GPS satellites determine a position on the planet, and the minimum coefficient of static friction for a ladder resting against a smooth wall. Answer parts (a) to (d).
Describe the process of compression moulding when used to manufacture aircraft components.
Answer as an ordered sequence of stages, from the charge being placed to the finished component being removed.
Include what the pressure step achieves: what does compression guarantee that a simple melt-and-fill process would not?
Explain the functions of a transistor in an electrical circuit.
There are two distinct functions to describe. For each one, say what goes in at the base and what comes out between the collector and the emitter.
Both functions rely on the same property — a small input controlling a large current — so make that the link between the two halves of your answer.
Outline how GPS satellites determine a position on the planet.
Work out who is doing the measuring: do the satellites calculate the position, or does the receiver?
A single distance from one satellite leaves a whole sphere of possible positions. Explain what extra information is needed to pin the position down to one point, and why that information is enough.
A uniform $8$-metre ladder with a mass of $12\,\mathrm{kg}$ has been placed against a smooth wall.
Determine the minimum coefficient of static friction between the ground and the ladder. Assume there is no friction between the ladder and the wall.
Take moments about the foot of the ladder. That reaction passes through the pivot, so it has no moment and your equation contains only the wall force and the weight.
The ladder is inclined, but the wall force is horizontal and the weight is vertical, so be careful which distances act as the moment arms. The coefficient then comes from $\mu = F/N$ at the point of slipping.

questions.text:
This question concerns roller coaster and aeronautical engineering: the shear force required by a punching die, the implications for the individual engineer and for the company when a design produced for the company is used without permission, and the internal forces in a loaded truss. Answer parts (a) to (c).
A component of a roller coaster car bogie is to be punched out from a $10\,\mathrm{mm}$ thick rectangular plate of mild steel as shown.
Calculate the shear force of the punching die if the shear stress is $345\,\mathrm{MPa}$.
The die does not fail across the face of the component — it shears the plate along the outline of the shape being punched out, so the shear area is a perimeter multiplied by the plate thickness.
The rounded ends must be added as arc lengths using the circumference formula for a circle, not treated as straight sides, and every length should be kept in millimetres until the area is converted to $\mathrm{m^{2}}$ for the stress calculation.
A team of engineers is working together to develop a new aeronautical device for a company. An engineer takes the design and produces the device without permission.
Describe the implications for the individual engineer and the company.
Split the response explicitly into the two parties — the individual engineer and the company — because marks are awarded for implications described for each.
Look for the ethical breach, the legal consequence, the effect on the company's development costs and profits, and any employment or health-and-safety consequence. Describe each implication; a list of headings with no description earns little.
A truss is loaded as shown.
Complete the table.
Before calculating, test each joint for zero-force members: at a joint with three members and no applied load, two of them are collinear, so the third carries nothing. That is often the shortest route to the first member.
For the second member, cut the truss so that only three members are crossed and take moments about the joint where the other two cross, leaving one unknown in the equation; summing vertical forces on the right-hand portion keeps the arithmetic simple.
Convert the loads consistently and remember that the diagonal members act at $60^{\circ}$, then state tension or compression from the sense of the assumed force.

questions.text:
Civil structures question set: piers, geotextiles, strap bracing and a tensioner drawing.
Two piers from different eras, used to support civil structures, are shown.
Outline how innovations in engineering materials have improved the in-service properties of piers.
The question is about what has changed between the two eras, not about which pier is stronger in the abstract.
Identify the property that has improved - durability, strength, resistance to insect attack, decay or environmental conditions. Naming a property earns a mark.
Then explain the mechanism or the treatment that produces the improved property, and give a consequence such as a longer service life or lower maintenance.
A geotextile used in the construction of a retaining wall is shown.
Explain why geotextiles are used in the construction of retaining walls.
Start with the fact that the fabric is permeable: water can pass through it. Ask what that does to the water trapped behind the retaining wall, and what it would otherwise do to the soil particles.
Then think about the backfill itself - the wall is pushing on a mass of soil, so ask whether anything in the wall changes how that soil behaves.
Aim for two or three distinct functions (drainage, separation, load distribution, reinforcement, erosion control), each explained rather than merely named.
Strap bracing is used in the construction of many residential structures. It has holes punched along its length to allow tensioners to be applied as shown.
A $6\,\mathrm{mm}$ diameter hole is to be punched into mild steel strap bracing.
If the shear strength of the bracing is $380\,\mathrm{MPa}$ and the shear force required to punch the hole is $5.73\,\mathrm{kN}$, what is the maximum allowable thickness of the strap bracing?
Punching a hole is a shear operation, and the shear area is the surface of material that has to be broken - think of it as the circumference of the hole multiplied by the thickness of the sheet.
Relate the average shear stress to the shear force on that area, being careful with units: the force is given in kN and the strength in MPa.
Solve for the thickness last, then check the result is a sensible value for sheet steel strap bracing - it should be well under a millimetre or two.
An orthogonal drawing of a strap brace tensioner is shown.
With reference to the orthogonal drawing and modified title block, complete the table.
Take the table one row at a time and decide whether each answer is read from the drawing itself or from the title block.
Two entries need interpretation rather than reading: the thread callout $M5\times0.8$ packs two separate pieces of information (what the prefix letter stands for, and what the second number measures), and the tolerance $R2.5\ \pm\ 0.5$ must be converted into the smallest and largest radii it permits.
For the line type, compare the three views: if one view omits a line type that the other two use to show internal or obscured detail, that is the answer.

questions.current_path: Year 12 / Aeronautical Engineering / Aerodynamics / define the responsibilities of the aeronautical engineer | Year 12 / Aeronautical Engineering / Aerodynamics / lift to drag ratio | Year 12 / Aeronautical Engineering / Aircraft systems and materials / computer graphics, computer aided drawing (CAD) | Year 12 / Aeronautical Engineering / Aircraft systems and materials / types including reinforced glass fibre, Kevlar, carbon fibre and Fibre Metal Laminate (FML) as used in aircraft construction
questions.text:
Aeronautical engineering question set: professional responsibilities, flight mechanics, CAD and aircraft materials.
Outline the environmental responsibilities of an aeronautical engineer.
This is a question about the engineer's obligations, not about the environmental impact of flying. Start from the law or the regulation - environmental protection legislation, workplace health and safety, and the airworthiness and noise regulations that apply to aircraft - and then state the duty that follows from it.
Two marks: one for a responsibility that genuinely belongs to the engineer (complying with the regulations that apply to the work, managing waste and hazardous materials, meeting design regulations for noise and emissions, selecting materials and processes with lower lifecycle impact) and one for a specific example tied to aeronautical work.
The mass of a single-engine propeller aeroplane, without pilot or passengers, is $906\,\mathrm{kg}$. It has a maximum lift to drag ratio of $10.5$. When fully loaded, the plane needs to produce $1050\,\mathrm{N}$ of thrust to maintain cruising speed and altitude.
What is the maximum total allowable mass for the pilot and passengers in kilograms?
The aeroplane is in level flight at constant speed, so it is in equilibrium: lift equals weight, and thrust equals drag. The thrust given in the question is therefore the drag.
The lift to drag ratio turns that drag into a maximum lift, and the maximum lift is the greatest total weight the aircraft can carry. Subtract the weight of the empty aeroplane to find what is left for pilot and passengers, and use the same value of $g$ for both weights when you divide.
Discuss the use of computer-aided drawing (CAD) in aeronautical engineering.
Write it as a discussion rather than a list: a benefit, the mechanism that produces the benefit, and then a limitation or trade-off. Three linked points earn more than three unconnected ones.
Look at how CAD is actually used in aircraft work: digital models driving prototypes, jigs and CNC tool paths; simulation and structural analysis of airframe bending, loads and fatigue, so a design weakness is found on screen rather than in flight; and the costs of the technology, being licence and hardware cost, the time to become proficient, and the risk of trusting a model in place of test data.
How does fibre metal laminate (FML) contribute to enhanced structural performance in aircraft?
FML is a laminate, not a single material: thin layers of aluminium with fibre layers (glass, carbon or aramid) bonded between them, so its properties come from how those layers cooperate.
Answer in terms of mechanisms, and compare with the aluminium alloy it replaces: how alternating stiff and tough layers stop a crack or a delamination from running; why isolating the metal layers reduces galvanic corrosion; how the fibre direction can be laid up to carry the load in the required direction; and what that means for mass, fatigue life and maintenance intervals.

Telecommunications engineers face many work health and safety risks while carrying out their duties.
With reference to ONE issue, describe strategies that can be implemented to reduce the risk for the engineer.
Choose ONE issue and state it clearly at the start, because every strategy you then describe must reduce that one risk.
Strategies can be engineering controls (change the equipment or the method), administrative controls (training, procedures, SWMS, signage, permits) and personal protective equipment - using strategies from at least two different levels is stronger.
Describe each strategy well enough that a reader can see how it lowers the likelihood or the consequence of harm, not just that it exists.
An orthogonal drawing of a wi-fi router is shown.

questions.current_path: Year 11 / Engineered Products / Materials and manufacturing / conduct simple tests aimed at improving materials’ properties through work hardening and heat treatment | Year 12 / Personal and Public Transport / Design and performance / investigate the principles and application of electric motors used in the transport industry, including motor speed control | Year 12 / Personal and Public Transport / Transport systems / basic calculations for work, energy and power | Year 12 / Personal and Public Transport / Design and performance / outline how changes in properties occur as a result of heat treatment processes
questions.text:
Personal and public transport question set: materials testing, electric motors, mechanics calculations and heat treatment.
How would impact testing be used during the design and development of a motorcycle helmet?
Start from the event the helmet protects against. The test has to reproduce a crash, so it must apply an impact at a known speed and measure what actually reaches the wearer's head.
For two marks, name what the test measures (energy absorbed by the shell and liner, peak deceleration at the headform, whether the shell is penetrated or fails, performance on off-centre impact) and then say how the result is used: it sets the shell thickness, liner density and materials during design, and it is the evidence of compliance with the relevant helmet standard before production tooling is committed.
Brushless DC motors are used to power electric-powered bicycles.
Why are these types of motors so well suited to this application?
Answer by pairing a property of the motor with a demand of an e-bike: the rider's power and the battery are both limited, hills need torque at low speed, and the motor lives on a vehicle that vibrates, gets wet and needs little maintenance.
A full response covers electronic (brushless) commutation giving efficient and precisely controlled operation, the absence of brushes meaning no wear, dust or servicing, high torque at low speed for starting and climbing, and compact, light construction. Regenerative braking is a bonus; efficiency, weight and size are what the question is really after.
An escalator is used to move people from the first floor to the second floor. The second floor is located $5.2\,\mathrm{m}$ above the first floor. The average person's mass is $64.8\,\mathrm{kg}$.
Determine the power requirement of the escalator in order to move 10 people from the first floor to the second floor in one minute.
This is a power question, so start with energy. Each of the 10 people gains gravitational potential energy $mgh$ on the way up, so the total energy gained is ten times one person's.
Power is energy divided by time, and the time is one minute expressed in seconds. Write the single-line calculation $P = \dfrac{10\,mgh}{t}$ and check that the units reduce to watts. Use one value of $g$ throughout and round to 2 or 3 significant figures.
Explain why a fully hardened steel would need to be tempered.
Support your answer with a labelled sketch of the resulting tempered microstructure.
Begin with the microstructure that causes the problem: after quenching, fully hardened steel is almost entirely martensite, a hard, supersaturated body-centred tetragonal phase, and the rapid quench also locks in high residual stresses. Hardness is what you want in a tool, but this structure is brittle and will crack.
Tempering is a second heat treatment carried out at a temperature below the critical point. Your sketch must show the end state of that treatment - small, evenly dispersed carbides in a continuous ferrite matrix, with both the particles and the matrix labelled - and not the needlelike martensite of the quenched condition, and not pearlite, because the treatment is stopped short of equilibrium.

Question set spanning aeronautical flight data recorders, a simple electrical circuit and pin-jointed truss analysis.
Outline how 'Black Box' flight data recorders have led to improved aviation safety.
The link between the recorder and safety is what happens after an incident, not what happens during the flight — think about who uses the data and what they are then able to do with it.
Keep the outline to the chain data recorded → cause identified → change made, and its effect on future flights. General statements about safety equipment do not earn the mark.
A circuit diagram is shown.
Use Ohm's Law to determine the current in the circuit.
Ohm's law applies to the equivalent resistance of the whole network, so reduce the circuit first: the two resistors connected across the supply are in parallel with each other, and that combination is in series with the remaining resistor.
Adding the conductances (or using the product-over-sum rule for the parallel pair) gives the total resistance, and only then does $I = V/R$ give the circuit current. As a check, the total must lie between the smallest and the largest individual resistance.
A pin-jointed truss is shown. Member $AB$ has been determined to be $250\,\mathrm{N}$ in compression.
Complete the table. You must use the method specified to solve each component.
Do the three rows in order and use the method named for each, starting with the external reaction because the member forces depend on it.
For the mathematical row take moments about the pin support so that only the roller reaction is unknown; for the sections row choose a cut that crosses CF plus two members meeting at a common joint, so that taking moments there leaves only CF; for the graphical row draw the force triangle to scale from the known member forces and measure the unknown side.
State the direction or the nature (T or C) with every value — the table asks for both, and the graphical answer should be quoted only to the precision the scale allows.

Outline ways in which satellite services have benefited people living and working in rural areas.
The key feature of satellite services is coverage: they do not depend on the user being near a terrestrial exchange or node, so they work where the cellular network does not reach.
For a 2-mark outline you need two genuinely different ways, not one idea explained twice.
Think about what changes for a rural school, hospital or farm compared with a metropolitan one: access to services, the cost of reaching them, and what infrastructure already exists there.
To avoid overloading a cellular network, a logic gate is used to control the activation of a signal booster.
The signal booster will only activate when both of the following conditions are met:
Complete a truth table for this scenario and identify a suitable logic gate.
Truth table:
Work out what a 1 and a 0 mean for each input column first, then fill the output column from the wording of the question rather than from the gate you think you need.
Look at which input combination produces an output of 1. The number of input states that give 1, and whether the inputs are used in their normal or inverted form, identifies the gate.
A useful check: a gate whose output is high only when every input is 0 is the inverse of a gate whose output is high when any input is 1.

Outline a method to protect against corrosion.

A towbar hitch is also exposed to abrasion and road salt, so a method that only keeps water off may not be the best choice. Only one method is needed, but it must be explained rather than named.

Think about what a shear pin has to do: carry the towing load in normal service and fail in a controlled way when the load is too high, so the property set needed is strength together with ductility rather than hardness alone.
Hot forging is a hot-working process in which the metal is plastically deformed above its recrystallisation temperature. The explanation must connect that to grain structure, strength and shape complexity, not simply assert that forging is strong.
